headline: Civilization is Humanity Hacking Brain's Computational Limits
summary: Discover how civilization's core algorithms, from bureaucracy to honor, are engineered to overcome the brain's cognitive constraints, and how digital infrastructure is set to revolutionize coordination.
details: What we call civilization is essentially a series of algorithms designed to solve the complex problem of coordinating more people than a single brain can track. This isn't a metaphor, but a technical description of how societies have scaled beyond small groups.

The human brain has a cognitive limit, approximately 145 monitorable social edges, known as Dunbar's Number. This neurobiological constant dictates that any group exceeding a certain size requires external coordination mechanisms to offload cognitive work.

Every known human society relies on five fundamental coordination algorithms: Bureaucracy (hierarchical command), Money and Taxation (decentralized routing), Moral Codes (default behavior), Family (high-trust connections), and Honor (distributed reputation).

These algorithms are structural solutions to the brain's finite processing capacity. Labels like communism vs. capitalism obscure the fact that all large organizations use the same foundational data structures.

The neoclassical model of the purely utility-maximizing individual fails in small groups where cooperative behavior emerges spontaneously. This empirical finding has significant implications for system design.

Proto-industrialization laid the groundwork for the Industrial Revolution by creating necessary infrastructure. We are now in an analogous 'proto-digitization' phase, poised for a complete remapping of the possibility space.

Digital infrastructure is beginning to bridge individual cognitive limits, making mechanism design—the engineering of incentive and coordination rules—a critical field. This marks a phase transition in how coordination can function.

The information-processing assumptions underlying classical algorithms are being invalidated by digital advancements, leading to a qualitative discontinuity in coordination possibilities. This is not gradual change, but a fundamental shift.

headline_marked: [[Miles Plug]] adds car tracking, crash detection, and AI mechanic for $99
headline: Miles Plug adds car tracking, crash detection, and AI mechanic for $99
summary: This new gadget plugs into your car's OBD-II port to monitor location, driving habits, and vehicle health, offering peace of mind for parents and drivers.
details: The Miles Plug is a new device designed to enhance car safety and monitoring. It plugs into a car's OBD-II port and offers features like crash detection, roadside assistance, location tracking, and a warning light decoder.

Developed by former Amazon (Ring and Blink) and Ubiquiti employees, the Miles Plug aims to provide parents with comfort, especially when teen drivers are on the road. The app shares trip and alert data with all family members, fostering trust.

The device costs $99, with a required membership for services. A one-year plan is $180 ($279 total), while a three-year plan is $396 ($11/month), paid upfront. It's compatible with most gas and hybrid cars from 2008 onwards, and some EVs.

Miles emphasizes user privacy, stating that vehicle, trip, and location data will never be sold. The app is ad-free, and sensitive data is end-to-end encrypted. Location tracking is tied to the car, not the phone, and stops when the driver leaves the vehicle.

The Miles app includes an AI chatbot called the Miles Mechanic, which can decode warning lights, assess urgency, and estimate repair costs. The app provides real-time alerts for speeding, hard braking, and trip summaries, alongside vehicle health information like engine status and battery levels.
